name: Mark Pawlikowski
title: Kill It and Watch It Come Back: Hands-on with Reliaburger
abstract:
I have never run a Kubernetes cluster. Yes, I said it.

Are you still with me? Cool!

Over the past last five years I talked to thousands of SREs and platform engineers at the conferences I run with my team: [SREday](https://sreday.com/), [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), [PLATFORMday](https://platformday.com/) and [Conf42](https://www.conf42.com/). 

The same story keeps coming back. Before the first container hits production you step into the world of Kubernetes, and then you need to build a whole team just to keep it running. A killjoy for many smaller teams. We started talking with my brother, [Miko Pawlikowski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mikolajpawlikowski/), how we could help the community ease some of these pains. 

Miko has been running platform teams on Kubernetes for 10+ years, leading him to start writing Reliaburger: one Rust binary with the scheduler, gossip, Raft, eBPF service discovery, ingress, mTLS, registry, metrics, logs, GitOps and chaos testing inside, driven by TOML. An app with health checks, ingress and autoscaling is twelve lines. He wrote the software. I am here to hand it to the community and see what you do with it.

This is a hands-on session, so bring a laptop (macOS on Apple silicon or Linux; Windows is not supported yet).

In 30 minutes you will:

1. Install Reliaburger with one command and start a node on your laptop. No container runtime, no root, no VMs: the built-in process runtime runs plain binaries.
2. Deploy an app from a twelve-line TOML file and watch it in the terminal dashboard and the web UI.
3. Ship a deliberately sick version and watch the health checker restart it, then roll back with one command.
4. Break it on purpose with the built-in fault injector: kill an instance, freeze another, and let `relish wtf` explain what just happened.
5. Read the manual and the source code from inside the binary, so you can keep going after the session.
6. Tell us what broke and what you liked.

Reliaburger is free and open source (Apache 2.0), and it is version 0.1, so it will break. That is where you come in. We are looking for helpers, burger ambassadors and contributors: people who will run it, break it, file the issues, write the docs and tell their teams. There are millions of practitioners running parts of Kubernetes they do not need, with more people than they should need to run it. We want this to become a community-driven project, just as our conferences are.
bio: Mark Pawlikowski runs SREday, LLMday and PLATFORMday, in-person conferences for the people who keep production up, and Conf42 online. He is not an engineer. He has spent the last five years listening to SREs and platform engineers describe what their work is actually like, and now brings Reliaburger, his brother Miko's batteries-included container orchestrator, to that community to play with, break and build on.

name: Jay Paulson
title: The Third Option
abstract:
When a major delivery is at risk, most organizations think they have two options: move the date or ask the team to take on more. In one large commerce platform, I found a third option.
I’ll walk through a real case involving 22 teams, 144 features, and a platform supporting roughly $32B in GMV. A Canadian rollout had already been delayed once. When new work put the timeline at risk again, another team was about five weeks ahead and had developed the skills to help. But that only mattered because the platform had been built with repeatable architectural patterns that made the work portable across team boundaries.
The delivery system made the option visible. The platform architecture made the option possible. I’ll show how those pieces came together, how I used them when the rollout was at risk, and what platform teams can learn from it when they design for more than developer experience.
bio: Jay Paulson is a Director of Engineering at Symetra with 25 years of experience across software engineering and technical leadership. His work focuses on platform architecture, predictable delivery, and building systems that give organizations better options when plans change. He has led large, multi-team product and platform initiatives with significant business exposure and is an Accredited Kanban Consultant.

name: Michael Angstadt
title: Multiplayer Agentic Software Development
abstract:
Coding agents work well for one developer. Building software with your entire cross-functional team and many agents creates a different problem: how do teams share context, avoid duplicate work, and keep decisions connected to the code?
This talk demonstrates how I managed this at ClosedLoop.AI through a real delivery workflow. We will show how teams share agentic components, use product and engineering intelligence to check scope, dependencies, and existing work, then carry those decisions through plans, issues, pull requests, and releases.
We will cover advanced topics like building a multiplayer session mesh, for communication between Claude Code and Codex sessions across people and machines and having agents can exchange durable messages through relays, coordinate work, and self-optimize sessions while they're running.
The result is a development process where human decisions remain clear, agent work stays connected, and useful context survives beyond a single terminal session.
bio:
Mike Angstadt leads engineering at Closedloop.ai, where his team builds tools for multiplayer software development with frontier AI agents. He is an engineering leader drawn to emergent technologies, hard product problems, and the new forms of productivity AI makes possible.
Over the last year, Mike and his team have focused on building faster without sacrificing quality with AI. They've achieved over 30× delivery increases per team member as they continue to discover the art of the possible.

name: Bradley Friemel
title: From Prototype to Production: Engineering AI Products That Last
abstract:
An impressive AI demo is only the beginning. Turning it into a product customers can depend on requires engineering decisions around reliability, evaluation, data access, cost, and integration with existing systems.
This talk explores AI productization from an engineering leader’s perspective, covering how to define useful product boundaries, evaluate unpredictable outputs, build observability and fallbacks, and balance delivery speed with operational confidence. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for moving beyond prototypes and shipping AI features that solve real customer problems, operate reliably, and deliver measurable business value.
bio: Bradley Friemel is a technology leader, former CTO, and startup founder with more than 15 years of experience building software products and leading engineering teams. His work bridges technical strategy, product development, and business outcomes, with a practical focus on turning AI capabilities into reliable, useful products. Drawing on experience across startups and private equity-backed businesses, Bradley brings a grounded perspective on AI productization: solving meaningful customer problems, building for scale, and measuring success through business value.
